blindSummary: This state/province is the only unit in the country — and the wider region — that has legislated the state of gender transition itself as a criminal offence. One provision of a 2026 religious-law bill, passed 12–13 August 2026, makes it an offence for a person bound by the state religion to change their own gender, cause another person's gender to be changed, or induce someone to do so, punishable by a fine of up to 3,000 units of local currency, imprisonment up to two years, or both; the bill also adds 'protection of modesty' decency provisions. The predecessor provision was actually used: in a case reported February 2026, this unit recorded its first prosecution for gender transition under a 2019 religious-law provision — a trans woman arrested by the state's religious-affairs enforcement department in an operation targeting a gathering of transgender individuals, heard at a local religious court; the national trans-rights monitoring group states this is the only state/province with such a provision. Critically, the country's highest court struck down 16 of 18 provisions of the 2019 enactment in February 2024 as outside state power; the state/province assembly resolved to re-enact them anyway, and did so in August 2026 — deliberate institutional commitment, not a stray provision. A foreign visitor who is, or is seen to be, of the state religion is squarely within the religious-law jurisdiction; a visitor of another faith is technically outside it but still exposed to the official climate the sequence creates.
blindSourceSummaries: A national newspaper (12 Aug 2026): previews the new religious-law bill replacing the 16 provisions of the 2019 enactment the country's highest court struck down — including 'protection of modesty' clauses making it an offence for a person of the state religion to fail to safeguard their private parts (whipping of 3-6 strokes plus a fine of up to 5,000 units of local currency or up to three years) alongside the clause criminalising gender change.

A national newspaper (13 Aug 2026): reports the state/province assembly passing the strict new decency rules of the religious-law bill — the enactment replacing the court-voided 2019 provisions, including the offence of gender change.

An independent outlet (4 Feb 2026): this state/province's first prosecution for the offence of gender transition under a 2019 religious-law provision (gazetted 2020) — a trans woman arrested by the state's religious-affairs department during an operation on a transgender gathering and charged under one provision (fine of up to 3,000 units of local currency or up to two years, or both), heard at a local religious court; the national trans-rights monitoring group's co-founder: 'Out of all the units, this one is the only that has this provision.' Believed the first case of its kind nationally, where sex-reassignment surgery is prohibited for adherents of the state religion except intersex people.

A national newspaper (9 Feb 2024): the country's highest court, by an 8-1 majority of a nine-member bench led by the chief justice, struck down 16 of 18 provisions of the 2019 religious-code enactment as beyond the state legislature's power because federal law covers the same offences — the ruling this state/province later legislated around.
blindTangential: The same 2026 bill's 'protection of modesty' provisions criminalise general moral and decency conduct for adherents of the state religion beyond gender transition — broad religious-law policing that reaches same-sex conduct and gender presentation as a category, not trans status alone.
